newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arabs ask U.S. to halt Israeli settlement drive.
newsitem.headline: Arabs ask U.S. to halt Israeli settlement drive.

text.p: Arab foreign ministers on Sunday asked the United States, as a sponsor of the Middle East peace process, to put financial pressure on Israel to stop settling Jews on occupied Arab territory.
The ministers, from Egypt, Syria and the six Gulf Arab states, made the appeal in a strongly worded statement that also criticised Iran for occupying three Gulf islands.
The Gulf states are the members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) -- Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

"The ministers...called on the United States to guarantee that American financial aid (to Israel) is not used in implementing the settlement policy," said the statement, issued after a two-day meeting in Cairo.
"They also urged the United States...to take necessary positions that would stop Israeli settlement expansion on occupied Arab lands," it added.

Relations with Syria -- and all of Israel's Arab neighbours -- have deteriorated over the Israeli government's commitment to expand Jewish settlements in the West Bank and other Arab lands captured in war.
Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq el-Shara told reporters on Saturday that the ministers were not optimistic about the fate of the peace process.
A White House spokesman has recently said Washington found the latest policy on settlements "a complicating factor" in peace efforts.

The ministers warned Israel it should not expect other states in the region to cooperate with it much until it withdraws from all occupied lands and allows the Palestinians to "attain their legitimate rights" -- listed in the statement as establishing a Palestinian state that includes Arab East Jerusalem.

"The ministers underlined their support to Lebanon and Syria in facing Israeli provocations and threats aimed at...imposing a fait accompli on the Arabs," the final statement said. It did not elaborate.
The eight countries, known as the Damascus Declaration states after the agreement they signed after the Gulf War in 1991, meet every six months to keep the alliance alive.
The next meeting will be held in the Syrian capital Damascus in June, 1997.
The ministers also denounced Iran for occupying three Gulf islands, controlled by Iran but claimed by the UAE.
They said Iran had deployed missiles on disputed Gulf islands and this was a direct threat to the Gulf Arab countries and again demanded that Iran withdraw from the islands.
The islands are Abu Musa, Greater Tunb and Lesser Tunb, which lie close to Gulf shipping lanes and which have been at the centre of dispute between the two Gulf states since 1992.
Other Arab states regularly support the UAE's claim to the islands but the statement on Sunday broke new ground in saying Iran had deployed missiles on them.

"The ministers repeat their demand that the Iranian government end its occupation of the three islands, refrain from practising a policy of imposing a fait accompli by force and stop building Iranian installations on the three islands with the aim of changing its demographic structure," it added.

The final communique also made general reference to the main goal of creating the alliance after the Gulf War in 1991 -- economic cooperation as a reward to Egypt and Syria for their role in the U.S.-led coalition that recaptured Kuwait from Iraqi forces.
